newsitem.title: GERMANY: Dell seen set for strong German growth.
newsitem.headline: Dell seen set for strong German growth.

text.p: Dell Computer Corp would surprise few in the personal computer industry if European sales show a dramatic rise when annual results are reported on February 25.
What should raise eyebrows is strong growth in Germany and France -- countries with sputtering economies and PC markets that have tripped up the direct-marketing pioneer in the past.

"Dell has really been a big success story this year and Europe has been no exception for them," said Chris Jones at market researcher Dataquest in Egham, England. "They exceeded the market growth rate in each country by far."

In 1996, Dell saw unit sales rise 84.3 percent in Germany, 75.4 percent in France and 39.3 percent Europe-wide, Jones said. For the same period, PC sales grew only about 11 percent in each of those markets, according to Dataquest.
In the first three quarters of Dell's 1997 business year, worldwide sales rose 43 percent to $2.02 billion and net income 92 percent to $145 million.
In Europe sales rose 41 percent to $482 million.

With units in the largest and third-largest European markets now set for growth, Dell expected European sales to rise about 30 percent annually for several more years, chairman Michael Dell said recently at the World Economic Forum.
"Germany and France are strategic markets for us," Hans-Juergen Mammitzsch, managing director of Dell Computer GmbH in Langen, told Reuters.
Germany in particular is ripe for gains because its once-formidable home-grown PC makers were weakening, Dataquest's Jones said.
In retail, Escom AG fell into bankruptcy last while Vobis Microcomputer AG expected 1996 sales to rise seven percent and pretax profit only one percent.
German leader Siemens Nixdorf Informationssystems AG barely turned a profit last year, while Peacock AG suffered a 20 million mark ($12 million) loss in 1995/96.

"Our business model is not dependent on development in the market," Mammitzsch said. "Our model is designed to take market share from competitors. We have some very tough local players, but I don't believe all of them will survive."
Dell would also step up the pressure later this year by allowing German customers to order PCs over the Internet.
"Speed is the key to our success, and we are really fast," said Mammitzsch, who joined Dell two years ago from Toshiba Corp's German PC unit.
"A customer on the Internet can have a sales proposal within minutes of hanging up the phone," he said.
Dell's direct business model, in which buyers order PCs built-to-order over the phone, has proved a success in Britain, where Dell is the number two PC vendor.
But previous forays into Germany and France floundered as its direct model struggled to win over those countries' credit-card shy customers.
Over the last three years, Dell has abandoned a failed move into retail sales, replaced its managers in Germany and France and added a twist to its direct approach: in-person sales calls.

"There are customers in Germany who feel more comfortable dealing with us in person," explained Mammitzsch. "After they see us and buy some of our products, then a lot of them start ordering over the phone."
Its renewed focus on selling to companies and experienced PC users also shielded it from the weak economies in France and in Germany, where 1996 home PC sales declined, Dataquest said.
"Corporate Germany is still seeing growth" in PC sales, Mammitzsch said. "The problem was the consumer side."

Dell's positioning avoids sales to novice users, who push up PC makers' costs by calling help centers early and often. "Right now the home market isn't profitable," Mammitzsch said. "It's a negative business."
